# Preface {.unnumbered}

These are the lecture notes for PHIL 444, Game Theory and Social Choice, at the University of Michigan.

They cover the game theory half of the course, and they stop where Sen starts. The second half works through Amartya Sen's *Collective Choice and Social
Welfare* [-@sen2017], and I'll do some notes for these, but I'm not going to do a book-like summary of a book..

Giacomo Bonanno's *Game Theory* [-@bonanno2024] is freely available online and is worth having open alongside these notes. It covers most of the same ground in a different voice, and it has 165 solved exercises, which these notes do not. Bonanno is by profession an economist not a philosopher (though he has published in philosophy journals, and is philosophically sophisticated), so he's naturally got a different emphasis at different points. And occasionally we disagree about the force of some consideration or other. But apart from differences in emphasis, the books mostly agree, and if you prefer his way of putting things (and over the years I've heard lots of students and GSIs say they learned a lot from his book), you should totally use it.

The notes began life in an older course, so the fit with what we are doing now is not exact. Where a section of the book is not on the schedule, it is there as background rather than as something you are expected to have read. (And the title of the book came from when it was meant to cover the whole of a course like this, not the first half.)

A PDF of the whole book is linked in the sidebar for anyone who would rather read it in one piece.

These notes arose from notes for various different courses (mostly at Michigan, but also at Rutgers and at St Andrews) over the years. I've received a lot of useful feedback on them, especially from faculty sitting in on the course at St Andrews, which has been incorporated into the notes. Before this term I ran the whole thing through Claude, to get advice on the prose and to see how it all fit together. It had many suggestions, both about the organisation and the prose, and about what needed to be added. I accepted a few of these suggestions in total, and many of them in part. It also chased down many of the references that I'd been cavalier about; I think I've double checked all of these, but I might have missed some.

The book is produced in [Quarto](https://quarto.org), using HTML and PDF templates that Claude built.
